topics.title: The 把 construction
topics.description: Putting the object first to talk about what you do TO it

guide.intro: 把 (bǎ) is one of the most distinctive features of Mandarin grammar. It moves the object before the verb to say "take X and do something to it". You'll hear it constantly — and English doesn't have a clean equivalent.

sections.text: The basic shape

Normal Chinese order is Subject–Verb–Object. With 把, you reorder to Subject–把–Object–Verb–(extra). The "extra" part is crucial — 把 sentences almost never end on a bare verb. There has to be a result, location, or change attached.

rows: 我 把 門 關 上
他 把 蘋果 吃 了
請 放 書 在 桌子 上
請 把 書 放 在 桌子 上

sections.text: When to use 把
Use 把 when you want to emphasize what HAPPENS TO a specific, known object — moving it, finishing it, changing it, putting it somewhere. Both speaker and listener know which object you mean.

rows.source: 我 把 作業 做 完 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.

rows.source: 請 把 窗戶 打 開。
他 把 杯子 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Tā bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le.

sections.text: If you can't say what HAPPENS TO the object, don't use 把. "我 把 蘋果 喜歡" is wrong — 喜歡 (like) doesn't change the apple.
What can't follow 把
把 needs a verb that physically affects the object. Verbs that don't qualify: feeling/perception verbs (愛, 喜歡, 覺得, 知道), existence verbs (有, 是), and most stative or motion-only verbs (來, 去, 走).

rows.source: 我 喜歡 這 本 書。
rows.translation: I like this book. (NOT 我 把 這 本 書 喜歡)

rows.source: 他 知道 答案。
rows.translation: He knows the answer. (NOT 他 把 答案 知道)

sections.text: Negation: 沒 / 不 goes BEFORE 把

rows.source: 我 沒 把 作業 做 完。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.

topics.title: The 被 passive
topics.description: When something happens TO the subject — usually unpleasantly

guide.intro: 被 (bèi) is the passive marker — "got / was done by". It's the mirror image of 把: where 把 puts the actor first and the patient mid-sentence, 被 puts the patient (victim) first.

sections.text: The basic shape
Pattern: Patient + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + result. The agent is optional — drop it if it's unknown or obvious.

rows.source: 我 的 手機 被 偷 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.

rows.source: 杯子 被 他 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Bēizi bèi tā dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: The cup was broken by him.

rows.source: 錢 被 老闆 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Qián bèi lǎobǎn ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: The money was taken by the boss.

sections.text: 把 vs 被 — same event, different POV

rows: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了
杯子 被 他 打 破 了
小偷 偷 了 我 的 手機
我 的 手機 被 (小偷) 偷 了

sections.text: Mandarin's 被 has a slightly negative or unfortunate flavor — it's used much more often for bad things (got stolen, broken, scolded) than for neutral or good ones. Sentences like "I was praised" (我 被 表揚 了) work but feel marked.
叫 / 讓 — informal alternatives
In speech, 叫 (jiào) or 讓 (ràng) often replace 被. They sound more casual — but unlike 被, they REQUIRE an agent.

rows.source: 我 的 錢 讓 他 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de qián ràng tā ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: My money got taken by him.

rows.source: 他 叫 老師 批評 了。
rows.translation: He got scolded by the teacher.

sections.text: Negation
Same as 把 — put 沒 BEFORE 被.

rows.source: 我 的 手機 沒 被 偷。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi bèi tōu.

sections.text: Two flavors of 了
Mandarin uses 了 in two distinct slots, and 把 / 被 sentences often need both. Knowing which is which is the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment.

rows: Something is now different / new situation

rows.source: 他 吃 了 三 個 蘋果。
rows.pinyin: Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
rows.translation: He ate three apples. (perfective 了₁ — action complete)

rows.source: 下 雨 了。
rows.translation: It's raining now. (sentence 了₂ — change of state, didn't use to be)

rows.source: 已經 下 了 三 天 雨 了。
rows.pinyin: Yǐjīng xià le sān tiān yǔ le.
rows.translation: It's been raining for three days. (BOTH 了 — completed duration AND ongoing relevance)

sections.text: Quick test: if the 了 hugs the verb (verb 了 object), it's 了₁. If the 了 is at the very end of the sentence, it's 了₂. Same character, different jobs.

topics.description: 給 as both "give" and a coverb meaning "for / to"

guide.intro: 給 (gěi) wears two hats. As a main verb it means "give". As a coverb sitting before another verb, it marks the recipient or beneficiary — "for someone", "to someone". Both uses are everywhere.

sections.text: 給 as main verb — "give"
Pattern: Subject + 給 + recipient + thing. Two objects in a row, recipient first.

sections.text: 給 as coverb — "for / to"
Sandwiched before another verb, 給 marks who benefits or receives the action. Pattern: Subject + 給 + recipient + verb + object.

topics.title: How well? — 得 complement
topics.description: Modify a verb with how it was done — 得 + adjective

guide.intro: 得 (de) lets you describe the manner or degree of an action: not WHAT you did, but HOW WELL or HOW MUCH. It's the closest Mandarin gets to English adverbs.

sections.text: The basic pattern
Pattern: Subject + Verb + 得 + (very) + Adjective. Note the position of 很 — almost always required to keep the sentence sounding natural.

rows.source: 他 跑 得 很 快。
她 唱 得 很 好。
我 睡 得 不 好。

sections.text: When the verb has an object
If your verb takes an object, you have to repeat the verb. Mandarin can't have an object AND a 得 phrase on the same verb. Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object, Verb + 得 + adjective.

rows.source: 他 說 中文 說 得 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: He speaks Chinese very well. (literally: "speaks Chinese, speaks very well")

rows.source: 她 寫 字 寫 得 很 漂亮。
rows.pinyin: Tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang.

sections.text: Common mistake: "他 說 中文 得 很 好" — wrong. The verb has to repeat. Or you can drop the object: "他 中文 說 得 很 好" also works.
Three different 得 / 的 / 地

rows: after a verb: how it was done
走 得 慢 — walks slowly

sections.text: All three are pronounced "de" (neutral tone) — only writing distinguishes them. Pay attention to position: 的 between nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.
Negation: not 不 before 得 — 不 before the adjective

topics.title: Verb complements
topics.description: Resultative & directional complements — what English handles with separate words, Mandarin stitches onto the verb.

guide.intro: English says "I looked but didn't see it" with two verbs. Mandarin says 我 看 了 但 沒 看見 — the result (見 = perceive) is glued to the verb (看 = look). This is the resultative complement, and it's everywhere. Directional complements work the same way but for motion.

sections.text: Resultative complements
Verb + result. The verb is the action you tried; the second character tells the outcome. Without the complement, you're only saying you DID the action, not that it WORKED.
Directional complements
Verb + direction. 上 (up), 下 (down), 進 (in), 出 (out), 回 (back), 過 (across). Compound forms add 來 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker): 上來, 下去, 進來, 出去 …

rows.source: 他 走 上 樓。
他 走 上 來 了。
她 跑 出 教室。
rows.translation: She runs out of the classroom.

sections.text: Potential complement: 得 / 不

To say you CAN or CAN'T achieve the result, insert 得 (able) or 不 (not able) between the verb and the complement: 看得見 / 看不見, 聽得懂 / 聽不懂. This is NOT the same as 可以 + verb — that asks for permission. Potential complements ask whether the result is achievable.
English speakers reach for 可以 看見 ("can see"). That's wrong. Use 看得見 ("see-able") for "I can see it".

topics.title: Measure word deep dive
topics.description: Beyond 個 — picking the right classifier for the noun: 條, 張, 只, 件, 把, 顆, 杯, 瓶 …

guide.intro: In A1 you learned 個 (the universal MW) and 本 (for books). Mandarin actually has hundreds of measure words — but you only need about a dozen to sound natural. The rule of thumb: shape and category of the noun pick the MW.

sections.text: Shape-based MWs

rows: fish, snakes, roads, pants, dogs (slim ones)

sections.text: Category MWs

rows: most animals; one of a pair

sections.text: Native speakers will understand if you say 一 個 魚 instead of 一 條 魚 — but you'll sound like a beginner. Picking the right MW is exactly what makes B1 sound like B1.
The 個 trap
English speakers over-use 個 because it's the safest fallback. Push yourself: when you see a long thin thing, reach for 條; flat → 張; clothing → 件; small round → 顆. Build the reflex.

lessons.title: 條 vs 張 — long vs flat
lessons.description: Shape decides — long-thin uses 條, flat-rectangular uses 張

exercises.prompt: Pick the right MW: 一 ___ 魚 (one fish)
exercises.explanation: Fish are long and slender → 條. 一 條 魚.

exercises.explanation: Tickets are flat sheets → 張. 三 張 票.

topics.title: Opinions & agreement
topics.description: I think, I believe, I agree — saying what you reckon

guide.intro: B1 means saying more than "I like" or "I want". You need ways to express opinions softly, agree, disagree, and ask people what THEY think. Three verbs do the heavy lifting: 覺得, 認為, and 看.

sections.text: 覺得 — feel / think (everyday)
覺得 (jué de) is the workhorse — "I feel / think that...". Use it for any soft, personal opinion. By far the most common in conversation.

rows.translation: I think this movie is good.

rows.source: 你 覺得 怎麼樣？

sections.text: 認為 — believe / hold (more formal)
認為 (rèn wéi) is firmer and more written — "I hold the view that...". Right for opinions on bigger issues, news, business, debate.

rows.source: 專家 認為 經濟 會 好轉。
rows.translation: Experts believe the economy will improve.

sections.text: 看 — see / view (informal opinion ask)
看 (kàn) literally means "look", but "你 看 …" idiomatically means "in your view, …". Used to gently ask someone's take.

rows.source: 你 看 我 該 怎麼 辦？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ kàn wǒ gāi zěnme bàn?
rows.translation: What do you think I should do?

rows.source: 我 看 應該 沒 問題。
rows.translation: I think it should be fine.

Chinese conversation tends to soften disagreement. "我 不 太 同意" (I don't really agree) is gentler and more common than a flat "不 同意".

topics.title: Telling a story
topics.description: Sequencing past events with 著 and directional verbs

guide.intro: When you narrate a story you need ways to set the scene ("she was sitting"), describe motion ("he walked in"), and string events together. 著 handles ongoing states; directional complements like 上來 and 下去 handle motion in space.

sections.text: 著 — ongoing state
著 (zhe) attached to a verb means "in the state of doing". It's NOT the same as English -ing — 著 emphasizes a held position or background condition, often setting the scene.

rows.source: 他 站 著。
rows.translation: He is standing. (in a standing state)

rows.source: 門 開 著。
她 笑 著 說。

sections.text: 著 vs 在: 在 means "actively doing right now" ("我 在 吃飯" — I'm eating). 著 means "in this state" ("門 開 著" — the door's open). For narration, 著 sets the scene; 在 reports a live action.
Directional complements: 上 / 下 / 進 / 出 / 來 / 去
Six little words combine into rich verbs of motion. Pair a base direction (up/down/in/out) with 來 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker).

她 跑 出去 了。
請 上來。

sections.text: Figurative directionals — 起來 / 下去 / 出來
Directional complements stretch beyond physical motion. Attached to non-motion verbs, they signal phase or aspect: starting, continuing, or coming-to-clarity.
